subChunks.title: Singleton & Factory Method
subChunks.hookHtml: Some objects should only exist once — a configuration store, a connection pool, a registry. Others should be created through a controlled gateway rather than scattered new calls. Singleton and Factory Method are the foundational patterns for managing object creation.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Singleton Pattern

Singleton ensures that a class has exactly one instance and provides a global access point to it.

class SpellRegistry {
    private static SpellRegistry instance;
    private final List<String> spells = new ArrayList<>();

    private SpellRegistry() {} // prevent external instantiation

    public static SpellRegistry getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {
            instance = new SpellRegistry();
        }
        return instance;
    }

    public void register(String spell) { spells.add(spell); }
    public void listAll() { spells.forEach(System.out::println); }
}

Every call to getInstance() returns the same object.

Thread Safety Concern

The basic lazy singleton is not thread-safe — two threads could both see instance == null and create two instances. Solutions include:

  • Eager initialisation: private static final SpellRegistry INSTANCE = new SpellRegistry();
  • Double-checked locking: check null, synchronise, check null again
  • Enum singleton: use a single-element enum — the JVM guarantees exactly one instance
// Safest Singleton — enum approach
enum SpellRegistry {
    INSTANCE;
    // ... methods
}

Factory Method Pattern

Factory Method delegates object creation to a static method (or overridable method), hiding the constructor behind a descriptive name.

class Spell {
    private final String name;
    private final int power;

    private Spell(String name, int power) {
        this.name = name;
        this.power = power;
    }

    // Factory methods — named, readable, can return subtypes
    public static Spell fireball() {
        return new Spell("Fireball", 80);
    }

    public static Spell withPower(String name, int power) {
        return new Spell(name, power);
    }
}

Spell s = Spell.fireball();
Spell custom = Spell.withPower("Blizzard", 70);

When to Use Each

  • Use Singleton for shared stateful resources: registries, caches, configuration
  • Use Factory Method when construction is complex, requires naming, or may return a subtype
  • Avoid Singleton for objects that could legitimately be tested in isolation — it makes mocking harder

storyBeats.text: The Academy's Spell Registry had been accidentally instantiated seventeen times — one per classroom, each with a different spell list. The Grand Audit revealed chaos. Eldrin convened an emergency lecture.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: One registry. One truth. The Singleton pattern exists because some objects are wrong in multiples. Make the constructor private, provide one gateway, and the Academy shares one authoritative record.

storyBeats.speaker: Code
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Be warned — in the multi-threaded Halls of Concurrency, the naive singleton is vulnerable. Prefer eager initialisation or an enum singleton when threads are at play.

storyBeats.speaker: Code
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And when construction needs a name — when 'new Spell(...)' is too blunt — give it a factory method. Spell.fireball() tells a story. Spell.withPower(name, 80) enforces rules before the object exists.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the Singleton pattern and why its private constructor is essential. Then explain why testing code that depends on a Singleton can be harder than testing code that receives its dependencies — and what pattern solves this problem.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A creational pattern ensuring a class has only one instance, with a global access point. One of the original Gang of Four patterns.
A thread-safe lazy Singleton technique: check null without locking, then lock, then check null again before creating the instance.
Using a single-element enum as a Singleton. The JVM guarantees exactly one instance per enum constant, even across serialisation and reflection.
A static method that returns an instance of the class, often replacing or supplementing public constructors with descriptive names.
An alternative to Singleton for managing shared objects — instead of global access, dependencies are passed in, improving testability.
The four authors of 'Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software' (1994), which catalogued 23 foundational patterns.
A category of design patterns (Singleton, Factory, Builder, Prototype, Abstract Factory) focused on object creation mechanisms.

questions.questionHtml: What is the purpose of making a Singleton's constructor private?
options: To prevent external code from creating additional instances
questions.correctAnswer: To prevent external code from creating additional instances
questions.explanationHtml: A private constructor means no external code (and no subclass) can call new ClassName(). All access to the instance must go through the controlled getInstance() method, enforcing the single-instance guarantee.
All three getInstance() calls return the same Counter object. Two increments on the same object give count = 2.

questions.correctAnswer: The constructor is public, so external code can still call new Registry() and create additional instances, breaking the Singleton guarantee. The constructor must be private.
questions.explanationHtml: Having a public constructor defeats the Singleton pattern entirely — any caller can create a new Registry with new Registry(). The constructor must be private so that only getInstance() can provide the single instance.

questions.questionHtml: A team has a Singleton DatabaseConnection. In unit tests they want to swap in a fake connection. Which approach best solves this?
options: Make the instance field public so tests can overwrite it
Add a reset() method that sets the instance to null
Inject the connection through a constructor or method parameter instead of using Singleton
Create a separate TestDatabaseConnection Singleton subclass
questions.correctAnswer: Inject the connection through a constructor or method parameter instead of using Singleton
questions.explanationHtml: Dependency Injection (passing the dependency in) makes the code testable — tests supply a fake implementation without touching global state. This is the core motivation behind DI frameworks like Spring. Singletons create hidden dependencies that are difficult to replace in isolation.

subChunks.title: Builder Pattern
subChunks.hookHtml: Imagine a class with six fields — some required, some optional, some with defaults. The constructor becomes a nightmare of parameters in the wrong order. The Builder pattern solves this with a fluent, readable API that makes object construction self-documenting.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Telescoping Constructor Problem

When a class has many optional fields, you end up with multiple constructors of increasing length:

// Unreadable — which 0 is power? which is duration?
new Spell("Arcane", 95, "Arcane", "Unstoppable force", 0, 3);

You lose track of parameter order, and optional fields must have defaults scattered across multiple overloads.

The Builder Pattern

A static inner Builder class constructs the object step by step. Each setter returns this (the builder), enabling chaining.

class Spell {
    private final String name;   // required
    private final int power;     // optional — defaults to 0
    private final String element; // optional
    private final String description;

    private Spell(Builder b) {
        this.name = b.name;
        this.power = b.power;
        this.element = b.element;
        this.description = b.description;
    }

    // Getters
    public String getName() { return name; }
    public int getPower() { return power; }
    public String getElement() { return element; }

    public static class Builder {
        private final String name; // required
        private int power = 0;
        private String element = "Neutral";
        private String description = "";

        public Builder(String name) { this.name = name; }

        public Builder power(int power) {
            this.power = power;
            return this;
        }
        public Builder element(String element) {
            this.element = element;
            return this;
        }
        public Builder description(String description) {
            this.description = description;
            return this;
        }
        public Spell build() { return new Spell(this); }
    }
}

Using the Builder (Fluent API)

Spell spell = new Spell.Builder("Arcane Surge")
    .power(95)
    .element("Arcane")
    .description("Unstoppable force")
    .build();

System.out.println(spell.getName());    // Arcane Surge
System.out.println(spell.getPower());   // 95
System.out.println(spell.getElement()); // Arcane

Required vs Optional Fields

Put required fields in the Builder constructor. Optional fields get setter methods with defaults. build() can validate before constructing:

public Spell build() {
    if (name == null || name.isBlank()) throw new IllegalStateException("Name required");
    return new Spell(this);
}

Builder vs Records

  • Use a record when all fields are required and known at creation time
  • Use a Builder when fields are optional, numerous, or when you want human-readable construction

storyBeats.text: The Spell Inscription Chamber was littered with failed castings — each one had been invoked with a seven-argument constructor, parameters in slightly the wrong order. The third argument was power, or was it duration? Nobody could remember.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: When construction requires many decisions, make each one explicit. The Builder pattern gives every parameter a name — and lets optional fields remain unset without a parade of null arguments.

storyBeats.speaker: Code
storyBeats.text:
Spell spell = new Spell.Builder("Arcane Surge")
    .power(95)
    .element("Arcane")
    .description("Unstoppable force")
    .build();

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The required fields go in the Builder's constructor — you cannot forget them. Optional fields have defaults. And build() is the moment of validation before the object is born.

storyBeats.speaker: Code
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Each setter returns 'this' — the builder itself. That is the secret of the fluent interface. The chain flows like a well-formed incantation from name to build.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Inside public class Main, implement a Spell class using the Builder pattern. Spell has four fields: name (String, required), power (int, default 0), element (String, default "Neutral"), description (String, default ""). Add getters for all four. The private constructor takes a Builder.

In main, build: new Spell.Builder("Arcane Surge").power(95).element("Arcane").description("Unstoppable force").build(). Print its name, power, and element on separate lines.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: A creational pattern that separates object construction from its representation, enabling step-by-step construction with optional parameters.
An API style where methods return the receiver (this), enabling method chaining that reads like a sentence.
An anti-pattern where a class has many overloaded constructors to handle combinations of optional parameters.
An object whose state cannot change after construction. Builders often create immutable objects by making all fields final.
A Java annotation from the Lombok library that automatically generates Builder boilerplate at compile time.
The build() method is the natural place to enforce invariants — throw IllegalStateException if required fields are missing or values are invalid.
A nested class declared static — it does not hold a reference to an outer instance, making it suitable for Builder which must be accessible before the outer object exists.

questions.questionHtml: Why does each setter in a Builder return this?
options: To allow the setter to access private fields
To create a new Builder copy per call
To satisfy the Java specification for builders
questions.explanationHtml: Returning this from each setter means the caller gets the same Builder back, allowing the next method call to be chained immediately: .power(80).element("Fire").build(). This creates a readable, self-documenting construction sequence.
The Builder is constructed with name "Rune", then qty is set to 5, then build() creates the Item. The Item fields are name="Rune" and qty=5, so the output is "Rune x5".

questions.correctAnswer: The name() and power() setter methods do not return 'this', so they return nothing (void is implied but the return type is declared as Builder). They must explicitly return 'this' to enable chaining.
questions.explanationHtml: Both setters declare a return type of Builder but have no return statement, causing a compile error. Each setter must end with return this; to pass the builder back to the caller for chaining.

questions.questionHtml: You have a class Wizard with two required fields and no optional fields. The fields are always provided together. Which construction approach is most appropriate?
options: Static factory method with six parameters
A no-args constructor with public setters
questions.explanationHtml: Builder shines when there are many optional fields or complex combinations. For a simple class with two required fields, a plain constructor or record is simpler, clearer, and more idiomatic. The Builder adds boilerplate without benefit here.
